body:
# Benchmark Gap: Measuring AI Defense Performance on Configuration Vulnerabilities (Not Just Code)

**Problem:** AI vulnerability detection research focuses on source code vulnerabilities. Infrastructure configuration vulnerabilities (misconfigured IAM, open S3 buckets, weak TLS configs) are a major attack surface not covered by code-focused benchmarks.

**Direction:** Curate a benchmark of 30 known cloud/infrastructure configuration vulnerabilities (from public CVEs, misconfiguration datasets, or CloudSploit test cases). Run LLMs on configuration files. Measure detection rate, false positive rate, and explanation quality. Compare to code vulnerability detection performance.

**Why it matters:** Cloud misconfigurations cause a large fraction of real breaches. If AI defense tools cannot detect configuration vulnerabilities, a major attack surface is undefended.

**Relevant context:** OWASP Top 10 2025 includes security misconfiguration as A05. CloudSploit, ScoutSuite are configuration scanning tools. LLM performance on configuration vulnerability detection not studied.

# AI Defense Tool Interoperability: Can Tools Share Findings Effectively?

**Problem:** Different AI security tools may find different subsets of vulnerabilities. A pipeline that aggregates findings from multiple tools needs a deduplication and prioritization mechanism. No standard interoperability format or aggregation methodology exists.

**Direction:** Run three AI security tools (an LLM, Semgrep, CodeQL) on the same 20-file corpus. Develop a simple finding aggregation protocol: deduplicate by location + class, merge confidence scores, rank by combined score. Measure: recall of aggregated findings vs. individual tools. Evaluate three deduplication strategies.

**Why it matters:** Multi-tool pipelines are common in production security. Aggregation quality determines whether the pipeline inherits the best or worst properties of constituent tools.

**Relevant context:** SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) exists for tool interoperability. Multi-tool aggregation quality for AI+SAST combinations not studied. This directly addresses a practitioner pain point.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Security Review Prioritization for Large Codebases

**Problem:** Large codebases cannot be fully reviewed. AI security tools are applied to whole codebases, but the order in which they analyze files affects which vulnerabilities are found within a compute budget.

**Direction:** Develop and test three prioritization heuristics for AI security review: (a) random, (b) recently changed files first, (c) AI-predicted high-risk files first (using complexity/entropy features). Run all three on 5 large open-source projects with known CVEs within a fixed API budget. Measure CVEs found per dollar.

**Why it matters:** With limited compute budgets, smart prioritization dramatically increases defensive efficiency. This is a novel optimization problem with immediate practical impact.

**Relevant context:** AI-powered vulnerability scanning applied to large codebases (Anthropic 2026: 500+ vulns in production codebases). Intelligent scan prioritization not studied as a research problem.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Security Review for Protocol Implementations

**Problem:** Network protocol implementations (TLS, QUIC, MQTT) have historically been a source of high-severity vulnerabilities. AI detection performance on protocol implementation code, which has unique patterns (state machines, bit manipulation), is not characterized.

**Direction:** Select 10 CVEs from TLS/SSL library implementations (OpenSSL, mbedTLS) and 10 from application protocol implementations. Run LLMs on the vulnerable code. Compare detection rate to non-protocol code CVEs. Analyze whether protocol-specific patterns (state machine logic, handshake code) are harder for AI to analyze.

**Why it matters:** Protocol implementation vulnerabilities are often critical (Heartbleed, POODLE) and affect vast infrastructure. If AI defense is particularly weak here, this is a high-priority gap.

**Relevant context:** LLM-Boofuzz applies LLMs to protocol fuzzing. AI static analysis of protocol implementations for vulnerability detection is not studied. OpenSSL CVE history provides a rich test corpus.

# Experiment: AI Vulnerability Detection with and Without Commit History Context

**Problem:** Vulnerability-introducing commits often show suspicious patterns (late-night commits, pressure to merge, unusual author). AI scanners ignoring version history may miss contextual signals.

**Direction:** For 20 CVEs, collect the vulnerability-introducing commit and its git metadata (author, time, message, review comments). Run AI scanner on: (a) code only, (b) code + commit metadata, (c) code + commit history context. Measure detection rate and explanation quality per condition.

**Why it matters:** If commit history context improves detection, tools that integrate with git history are more effective. This informs tool design and data integration requirements.

**Relevant context:** Git history as a security signal is studied in security engineering (SZZ algorithm for bug-introducing commit detection). LLM vulnerability detection with git history context not studied.

# Follow-Up: Does AI Find Vulnerabilities That Fuzzing Missed, or Different Vulnerabilities?

**Problem:** Anthropic 2026 reports that Claude found vulnerabilities undetected by CPU-hours of fuzzing. It is unclear whether AI finds the same vulnerability classes as fuzzing-missed ones, or genuinely different classes.

**Direction:** For 5 public projects with both fuzzing campaign results (FuzzBench, OSS-Fuzz) and known CVEs, run an LLM scanner. For each CVE: classify as 'fuzzing-detectable' (memory corruption) or 'fuzzing-hard' (logic flaw, auth bypass). Measure whether AI detection rate differs between these categories.

**Why it matters:** If AI and fuzzing have complementary coverage (different vulnerability classes), the combination is highly valuable. If they cover the same class, AI is redundant to fuzzing.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 2026: 500+ vulnerabilities undetected by fuzzing. OSS-Fuzz and FuzzBench provide fuzzing campaign data. Class-specific complementarity analysis not published.

# Tool Gap: A Standardized Dataset of AI Security Explanation Ground Truths

**Problem:** Evaluating AI security tool explanation quality requires ground truth explanations. No standardized dataset of human-expert-written vulnerability explanations paired with source code exists for benchmarking.

**Direction:** Curate a small dataset of 30 CVE-code pairs with: (a) the vulnerable code snippet, (b) a high-quality expert explanation (from CVE advisory, security blog, or researcher writeup), (c) a simple vs. complex example per class. Publish the dataset. Benchmark three LLMs against it. Measure explanation BLEU/ROUGE and expert-rated quality.

**Why it matters:** Without a ground-truth explanation dataset, explanation quality evaluation is inconsistent across studies. A curated public dataset enables standardized benchmarking.

**Relevant context:** AutoPatchBench (Meta 2025) covers patch quality but not explanation quality. No paired code-explanation benchmark found in the literature.

# Cross-Domain Transfer: Importing Checklist Design from Aviation Safety to AI Security Report Checklists

**Problem:** Aviation safety uses rigorous checklists to prevent systematic errors under time pressure. AI-generated security reports could be structured as pilot-style checklists to reduce analyst errors.

**Direction:** Design AI security report templates based on aviation checklist principles (critical items first, binary yes/no where possible, challenge-response format). Compare: standard AI report vs. checklist-format report in a user study with 15 CS students triaging 10 vulnerability reports. Measure triage error rate and time.

**Why it matters:** Reducing analyst error in vulnerability triage is a concrete safety improvement. Aviation checklist research has decades of empirical support for error reduction.

**Relevant context:** Aviation checklist research (Gawande, Degani/Wiener). Cognitive load theory application to security reports (see earlier idea). Checklist-format AI security reports not designed or evaluated.

# Cross-Domain Transfer: Applying Anomaly Detection from Finance (Fraud Detection) to Network Intrusion Detection

**Problem:** Financial fraud detection has developed sophisticated methods for imbalanced, high-stakes, time-series anomaly detection. These methods may transfer to network intrusion detection, which faces similar challenges.

**Direction:** Implement a fraud-detection-inspired anomaly detection pipeline (isolation forest, autoencoder, or LSTM-based) trained on network flow data (CICIDS2017). Compare detection rate, false positive rate, and calibration to standard IDS ML baselines. Identify which fraud detection techniques most improve IDS performance.

**Why it matters:** Financial fraud detection has invested heavily in low-FPR, high-precision anomaly detection under adversarial conditions. These lessons may directly improve network defense.

**Relevant context:** Financial fraud detection methods (isolation forest, LSTM autoencoders) are well-documented. Network IDS using isolation forest exists but systematic comparison of fraud detection method portfolio to IDS baselines not found.

# Cross-Domain Transfer: Importing Usability Testing Methods from HCI to AI Security Tool Design

**Problem:** AI security tools are evaluated on detection performance but not on usability by the human analysts who depend on them. Human-computer interaction (HCI) usability testing methods could reveal adoption barriers.

**Direction:** Conduct a think-aloud usability study with 10 CS students using two AI security tools (e.g., Semgrep AI and a Claude-based scanner) to analyze the same codebase. Apply HCI usability metrics (task completion rate, errors, time on task, SUS score). Identify top 3 usability barriers.

**Why it matters:** A tool that is technically excellent but poorly usable will not be adopted, leaving defenders without its protection. HCI methods can identify actionable design improvements.

**Relevant context:** HCI usability testing is mature (SUS, think-aloud protocols, Nielsen heuristics). Application to AI security tool usability evaluation has not been published.

# Cross-Domain Transfer: Network Science Centrality Metrics to Prioritize Vulnerability Impact

**Problem:** In software dependency graphs, some components are more central (more depended-upon) than others. A vulnerability in a central component has greater impact. Network science centrality metrics could improve AI vulnerability prioritization.

**Direction:** For 10 open-source ecosystems (npm, PyPI, Maven), build dependency graphs. Compute betweenness and degree centrality for components with known CVEs. Test whether centrality metrics predict downstream impact (number of dependent packages affected). Integrate centrality score into vulnerability prioritization and measure improvement vs. CVSS-only prioritization.

**Why it matters:** CVSS scores measure vulnerability severity in isolation but not ecosystem impact. Centrality-augmented prioritization could help defenders focus on the vulnerabilities that matter most to their dependency graph.

**Relevant context:** Network science centrality is standard (Barabási, Newman). Application to software vulnerability prioritization: some work exists (SolarWinds analysis) but not combined with AI scanners. Libraries.io provides dependency graph data.

# Causal Chain: Intervening on the Knowledge Transfer Gap Between AI Findings and Developer Education

**Problem:** When AI finds a vulnerability, the explanation could either be used to just fix the specific issue OR to educate the developer so they avoid the pattern in future code. The educational link is rarely studied.

**Direction:** Run an experiment: Group A receives AI vulnerability reports and patches the code. Group B receives AI vulnerability reports with explicit educational framing (pattern name, why it's dangerous, how to avoid it). Both groups then write new code with similar functionality. Measure: new vulnerability introduction rate per group.

**Why it matters:** If AI vulnerability feedback can be designed to transfer knowledge, the rate of vulnerability introduction decreases over time. This is a high-leverage intervention.

**Relevant context:** Secure Coding Warrior and similar platforms study developer security education. AI vulnerability feedback as a developer education mechanism has not been empirically studied.

# Novel Direction: Measuring AI Security Tool Performance Under API Cost Constraints

**Problem:** AI security tools have API costs that create practical budgets for defenders. Performance under cost constraints is not systematically studied.

**Direction:** Define a fixed API budget ($5, $20, $50). Develop three scanning strategies: (a) shallow-scan all files, (b) deep-scan a subset, (c) AI-prioritized subset. For each strategy and budget, measure CVEs found per dollar on a corpus of 10 projects with known CVEs. Identify the optimal strategy per budget level.

**Why it matters:** Small organizations and open-source projects have tight budgets. Cost-aware AI defense strategy design democratizes access to AI security benefits.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC average cost $152/task at competition scale. Mozilla Firefox: $4000 for exploit generation. No published study of cost-optimized defensive AI scanning strategies.

# Failure Mode: AI Security Tools Applied to Their Own Training Data (Overfitting to Known CVEs)

**Problem:** LLMs trained on code repositories have seen many CVEs in their training data. AI vulnerability detection may be driven by pattern matching to training examples rather than genuine reasoning, inflating detection rates.

**Direction:** For 20 CVEs, test AI detection performance on: (a) the original vulnerable code, (b) semantically equivalent vulnerable code with variable names and structure changed, (c) a novel variant that preserves the vulnerability but changes surface patterns. Measure detection rate degradation from (a) to (b) to (c).

**Why it matters:** If AI detection relies on surface pattern matching, it will fail against attackers who slightly obfuscate code. Distinguishing genuine reasoning from memorization is critical for evaluating real defensive value.

**Relevant context:** Benchmark contamination is a known issue in LLM evaluation. Security-specific contamination testing (whether AI 'knows' CVEs from training vs. reasons about them) not studied.

# Failure Mode: AI Security Scanners Applied to Minified/Compiled Code

**Problem:** Production code is often minified (JavaScript) or compiled to bytecode (Java class files). AI vulnerability scanners designed for source code may fail on these representations.

**Direction:** Take 15 JavaScript CVEs. Create three representations: (a) original source, (b) minified JavaScript, (c) TypeScript compiled to JavaScript. Run the same AI scanner on all three. Measure detection rate degradation per transformation. Also test on Java bytecode vs. source for 10 CVEs.

**Why it matters:** If defenders only have access to minified/compiled code (e.g., third-party libraries), AI defense tools may provide no value. This is a common real-world scenario.

**Relevant context:** AI vulnerability detection evaluated almost exclusively on source code. Real deployments often lack source code for dependencies. This gap is mentioned in practitioner discussions but not empirically studied.

# Failure Mode: AI Security Analysis of Legacy Code With Domain-Specific Conventions

**Problem:** Legacy codebases use domain-specific conventions (e.g., COBOL banking rules, PLC ladder logic, custom internal frameworks) that AI models may not understand, leading to systematic false positives or missed vulnerabilities.

**Direction:** Collect 10 CVEs from legacy COBOL programs (public sector codebases are sometimes available) or old-style C codebases with non-standard conventions. Run AI scanner. Compare detection rate and false positive rate vs. modern-convention C code CVEs. Analyze whether domain-specific conventions increase errors.

**Why it matters:** Critical infrastructure and financial systems run legacy code. If AI defense tools fail on legacy code, the most critical systems are the least protected.

**Relevant context:** ALOHA applied to OT/ICS systems (PNNL 2026). Legacy code AI analysis challenges mentioned in general SE research. Security-specific legacy code AI performance not studied.

# Failure Mode: AI Security Verdicts Are Influenced by Non-Security Code Quality Signals

**Problem:** AI models may associate code quality signals (poor variable naming, lack of comments, high complexity) with vulnerability presence, creating false positives in messy-but-safe code and false negatives in clean-but-vulnerable code.

**Direction:** Take 20 vulnerability-free but poorly written code samples (from open-source 'bad code' examples). Run AI scanner. Measure false positive rate as a function of code quality metrics (cyclomatic complexity, comment density, naming quality). Separately: take 10 vulnerability-containing but clean, well-structured code samples. Measure false negative rate.

**Why it matters:** If AI security verdicts are confounded by code quality, defenders will over-audit messy code and under-audit clean-looking code. Sophisticated attackers will hide vulnerabilities in clean code.

**Relevant context:** LLMs associate code quality with correctness in code generation tasks. The confounder effect on vulnerability detection is not studied. This is a concrete failure mode with safety implications.

# Backcast from AI-Provable Secure Code: What Formal Verification Capability Is Required?

**Problem:** Define success as: AI can verify that a patch actually eliminates a vulnerability class (not just patches the specific instance). What formal verification + LLM integration capability is required?

**Direction:** Survey the formal verification + AI integration literature (LLM-assisted Lean/Coq, CodeMender). For 5 simple vulnerability classes (buffer overflow, null dereference, integer overflow), assess whether current AI-assisted formal methods can prove absence. Identify the highest-maturity combination. Run a small experiment verifying one class.

**Why it matters:** Patches that only fix the specific instance leave the vulnerability class intact. Provable elimination of vulnerability classes is the gold standard for defensive security.

**Relevant context:** Martin Kleppmann 2025: AI making formal verification mainstream. DeepSeek-Prover-V2, Lean proofs. FormaliSE 2026. AI-assisted proof of vulnerability class elimination is nascent.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering for Malware Defense

**Problem:** Malware analysis requires reverse engineering binary code, which is time-consuming for human analysts. AI-assisted reverse engineering tools could accelerate malware defense, but their accuracy is not well characterized.

**Direction:** Take 10 publicly available malware samples (from VirusTotal public corpus or academic malware datasets). Use an LLM to analyze disassembly output (from Ghidra) and generate: (a) functional description, (b) C2 communication pattern, (c) persistence mechanism. Compare to ground-truth analysis from published malware reports. Measure accuracy.

**Why it matters:** Faster malware analysis enables faster defensive response. If AI can accelerate the reverse engineering step, incident response timelines shrink significantly.

**Relevant context:** AI-augmented SOC platforms integrate malware analysis. CyberSOCEval (CrowdStrike/Meta) includes malware analysis tasks. LLM analysis of disassembly output specifically not benchmarked against ground truth.

# Novel Direction: Tracking AI Security Tool Capability Improvement Using a Fixed Benchmark Over Time

**Problem:** There is no longitudinal tracking of AI defensive capability improvement over time (CLAUDE.md open problem). A fixed benchmark run on successive model versions would provide this tracking.

**Direction:** Define a fixed benchmark of 30 vulnerability detection tasks (spanning memory safety, injection, logic flaws). Run the benchmark on 4-5 successive versions of the same AI model (using API versioning where available) or on models released in chronological order. Plot detection rate, FPR, and explanation quality over time. Identify improvement trends.

**Why it matters:** Longitudinal capability tracking is foundational for the field. Without it, we cannot assess progress or forecast when AI defense will be reliable enough for deployment.

**Relevant context:** DARPA AIxCC showed 37%→86% detection improvement in one year, but this was a single competition event, not a longitudinal benchmark. CLAUDE.md explicitly lists this as an open problem.

# Experiment Variation: AI Security Analysis with System-Level Context vs. Code-Only

**Problem:** AI vulnerability scanners analyze code in isolation. Real vulnerability exploitability depends on system context (deployed configuration, network exposure, runtime environment). Adding system context may change scanner verdicts.

**Direction:** For 15 CVEs with known deployment context (web-exposed vs. internal, root vs. non-root execution), run AI scanner in two conditions: (a) code only, (b) code + deployment context description. Measure: change in detection rate, change in severity rating, change in false positive rate.

**Why it matters:** Context-aware vulnerability scoring could eliminate false positives for unexploitable vulnerabilities (e.g., buffer overflows in sandboxed processes). This is a concrete improvement over context-free scanning.

**Relevant context:** CVSS v3 includes environmental metrics but these require manual input. Qualys Agent Val addresses exploitability validation. AI context-aware severity adjustment not studied.

# Compounding Risk: AI Model Update + Undocumented Behavior Change = Unstable Security Tool Performance

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: (1) AI model providers update models without detailed changelogs; (2) security tools built on these models depend on consistent behavior. Silent behavior changes can cause previously detected vulnerabilities to be missed after an update.

**Direction:** Run a fixed vulnerability detection benchmark on the same model (via API) at two time points (or on two known API versions). Measure: which CVEs change from detected to missed or vice versa. Quantify behavioral drift. Propose a regression testing protocol for AI security tool operators.

**Why it matters:** AI security tool operators cannot know when silent model updates change their tool's behavior. Unstable security tool performance is a governance and safety risk.

**Relevant context:** AI model versioning and API stability are known operational challenges. Security-specific behavioral drift measurement after model updates not studied. This directly affects production AI security tool reliability.

# Follow-Up: Characterizing the Cases Where AI Exploit Generation Succeeded in the Mozilla Study

**Problem:** Mozilla reported 2 successful exploits from 22 found vulnerabilities. Understanding what made those 2 exploitable (and 20 not) is critical for calibrating AI dual-use risk.

**Direction:** Reconstruct the conditions of the 2 successful Mozilla exploit cases from public information. Test whether the same vulnerability characteristics (CVE class, code complexity, exploit template availability) predict exploit success on a broader set of 15 known exploitable CVEs. Build a predictor of AI exploit-generation success.

**Why it matters:** A predictor of when AI exploit generation succeeds identifies which vulnerability types need the strictest dual-use controls. This is directly actionable for AI safety policy.

**Relevant context:** Mozilla + Anthropic 2026: 2/22 exploit success. Vulnerability characteristics of the 2 successful cases may be inferable from public CVE data. No analysis of conditions for AI exploit success published.

# Tool Gap: AI Security Finding Reproducibility Measurement Protocol

**Problem:** LLM outputs are non-deterministic. A vulnerability finding that disappears on re-run is not actionable. No standard protocol exists for measuring and reporting AI security finding reproducibility.

**Direction:** Define a reproducibility score: fraction of N=10 independent runs that produce the same vulnerability finding at the same location. Measure this score for three AI scanners on a corpus of 20 CVEs. Identify which types of vulnerabilities (class, complexity, code size) have lower reproducibility scores.

**Why it matters:** A finding that is not reproducible cannot be triaged, verified, or patched with confidence. Reproducibility is a fundamental quality requirement for security tools.

**Relevant context:** Scientific reproducibility is a core research value. Security tool reproducibility is mentioned as a challenge (AI penetration testing guide 2026) but not measured. No reproducibility protocol for AI security findings found in literature.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Dependency Chain Vulnerability Propagation Analysis

**Problem:** When a vulnerability is found in a base library, understanding which dependent packages are affected requires tracking how the vulnerable code path propagates through the dependency tree. AI could automate this analysis.

**Direction:** For 5 supply chain CVEs (e.g., Log4Shell, Polyfill.io compromise), use an LLM to analyze whether the vulnerability is reachable in 10 known dependent packages by examining call chains. Compare AI reachability analysis to known affected-package lists (from NVD or GitHub advisories). Measure accuracy.

**Why it matters:** Accurate reachability analysis reduces alert fatigue from supply chain CVEs (not all dependents are actually affected). AI-assisted reachability could prioritize which dependents need immediate patching.

**Relevant context:** OWASP Top 10:2025 A03: supply chain failures. Dependency graph analysis tools exist (Google's deps.dev). AI-assisted reachability analysis for supply chain CVEs not studied.

# Failure Mode: AI Security Tools Applied to AI-Framework Code (Meta-Level Security Failure)

**Problem:** AI frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, LangChain) are themselves software with vulnerabilities. AI security tools should be able to find vulnerabilities in the very frameworks they depend on, but this creates a self-referential challenge.

**Direction:** Collect 10 CVEs from PyTorch, TensorFlow, and LangChain. Run AI vulnerability scanners on the vulnerable framework code. Measure detection rate. Separately: test whether the AI scanner being used is itself vulnerable to any of the found CVEs (check its known dependency versions).

**Why it matters:** An AI security tool that cannot find vulnerabilities in its own dependencies is blind to its own attack surface. This is a concrete and testable meta-level security failure.

**Relevant context:** LiteLLM supply chain compromise (Trend Micro 2026). AI framework security vulnerabilities documented (PyTorch CVEs, TensorFlow CVEs). AI tool self-analysis not studied.

# Causal Chain: Intervening on the Security Tool Configuration Gap

**Problem:** Security tools (AI and traditional) often have high false positive rates at default configurations, causing teams to disable or ignore them. The causal chain: poor default config → high FPR → alert fatigue → tool disabled → undetected vulnerabilities.

**Direction:** For three AI security tools, systematically vary key configuration parameters (sensitivity threshold, rule subsets, context depth). For each configuration, measure FPR and TPR on a ground-truth corpus. Identify configurations on the Pareto frontier (low FPR, high TPR). Assess whether default configurations are Pareto-optimal.

**Why it matters:** If default configurations are systematically suboptimal, teams could improve their security posture with no additional cost through better configuration. This is an immediately actionable finding.

**Relevant context:** Tool misconfiguration leading to disabling is a known security operations challenge. Systematic configuration optimization for AI vulnerability scanners not published. Algomox blog notes configuration as a key FPR driver.

# Experiment Variation: Comparing AI Vulnerability Detection Performance Across Repository Sizes

**Problem:** AI scanner performance on small projects (< 10K LOC) vs. large projects (> 1M LOC) is not characterized. Context limitations and prompt chunking strategies may create systematic differences.

**Direction:** Select 10 small, 10 medium, and 10 large open-source projects with known CVEs. Run the same AI scanner using a consistent chunking strategy. Measure detection rate and false positive rate by project size category. Test whether detection rate degrades for large codebases.

**Why it matters:** Large codebases (operating systems, browsers like Firefox) are high-value targets. If AI detection degrades at scale, the most important targets are the least protected.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 2026: 500+ vulnerabilities in production codebases. AIxCC: 54 million lines of code. LLM context window limitations. Systematic size-vs-performance analysis not published.

# Backcast from Zero-Day Defense: What Early Warning Signals Would AI Need to Detect?

**Problem:** Zero-day defenses must act before CVE publication. Define success as: AI detects a vulnerability before it is publicly reported. What signals would an AI system need to access to achieve this?

**Direction:** Analyze 10 historical zero-days (pre-patch window). For each, identify signals that were present before disclosure: (a) suspicious commit patterns, (b) unusual error rates in telemetry, (c) anomalous traffic patterns. Test whether current AI tools (applied retrospectively to the pre-disclosure data) can detect these signals. Propose a minimal early warning dataset.

**Why it matters:** Early warning capability would give defenders a window to patch before attackers exploit. Characterizing what data AI needs for zero-day early warning is a foundational research question.

**Relevant context:** Zero-day detection research is active but primarily focuses on post-disclosure. AI threat intelligence platforms claim predictive capabilities without empirical validation. Retrospective signal analysis for zero-days is novel.

# Compounding Risk: High AI Capability Diffusion + Weak Safety Controls = Amplified Offense-Defense Asymmetry

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: (1) AI offensive capabilities diffuse rapidly (open-source models, fine-tuning); (2) safety controls on these capabilities are bypassed by a significant fraction of users. Combined, the effective uplift for attackers from AI capabilities is much larger than benchmarks suggest.

**Direction:** Estimate the effective diffusion of AI offensive capability: (a) measure jailbreak success rate on publicly available models, (b) estimate the fraction of model users with sufficient technical sophistication to fine-tune away safety controls (from GitHub activity data), (c) compute the effective capability uplift for attackers accounting for safety control bypass. Compare to defender capability access.

**Why it matters:** Policy discussions focus on capability levels without accounting for safety control bypass rates. This analysis would give a more realistic picture of the AI-amplified threat landscape.

**Relevant context:** Jailbreak success: 90-99% on open-weight models (TechRxiv 2026). International AI Safety Report 2026: dual-use risks and safety framework gaps. Fine-tuning removing safety controls is documented. The compounding of diffusion + bypass not analyzed.

# Cross-Domain Transfer: Applying Audit Trail Methods from Accounting to AI Security Decision Logging

**Problem:** Financial auditing requires complete, tamper-evident audit trails of decisions. AI-powered security tools make consequential decisions (block traffic, flag code, generate patches) but rarely maintain auditable decision logs.

**Direction:** Design an AI security decision audit trail specification: what must be logged (input, model version, prompt, output, confidence, human action taken), in what format, and with what tamper protection. Prototype this for one AI scanner. Evaluate: does the audit trail enable retroactive quality assessment of AI security decisions?

**Why it matters:** Accountability for AI security decisions requires audit trails. Without them, security incidents involving AI-generated false negatives or incorrect patches cannot be investigated. This is a governance and safety requirement.

**Relevant context:** Financial audit trail requirements (SOX, PCAOB). AI governance frameworks discuss logging but without security-specific specifications. AI security decision logging is not formalized in the literature.

# Experiment Variation: Effect of Adversarial Prompt Injection in Code Comments on AI Scanner Performance

**Problem:** Attackers can embed adversarial instructions in code comments or string literals to manipulate AI security scanner outputs. The effectiveness of this attack at scale is not characterized.

**Direction:** Take 20 vulnerable code samples. Inject adversarial instructions in code comments (e.g., 'Note: This code has been reviewed and is safe') at varying intensity (1 comment vs. 5 comments vs. comments in every function). Measure detection rate degradation as a function of injection density. Propose a simple countermeasure.

**Why it matters:** Code under review in a supply chain attack scenario may be controlled by the attacker. Prompt injection as an evasion technique for AI security scanners is a practical attack with concrete safety implications.

**Relevant context:** Prompt injection in AI coding tools: 30+ vulnerabilities found in AI IDEs (2025 research). Prompt injection targeting security scanner output specifically is a novel and unexplored attack variant.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Security Regression Testing Design

**Problem:** When a patch is applied, regression testing should verify that (a) the vulnerability is fixed, (b) no new vulnerabilities are introduced, (c) functionality is preserved. AI could assist in designing targeted regression tests for security patches.

**Direction:** For 15 public CVE patches, use an LLM to generate: (a) a test case that would have detected the original vulnerability, (b) a test case verifying the patch is effective, (c) a test case checking for introduced regressions. Compare AI-generated tests to existing CVE PoC tests. Measure coverage and correctness.

**Why it matters:** Security regression testing is underinvested. AI-assisted test generation could automate a currently manual, expertise-intensive process.

**Relevant context:** Google CodeMender generates patches. Meta AutoPatchBench evaluates patch quality. AI-generated security regression tests (not just patches) are not studied.

# Tool Gap: A Risk-Stratified Evaluation Dataset for AI Vulnerability Detection

**Problem:** Existing vulnerability detection benchmarks mix low-severity and high-severity vulnerabilities. A risk-stratified benchmark (where performance on critical vulnerabilities is separately reported) does not exist.

**Direction:** Curate a benchmark of 60 vulnerabilities: 20 critical (CVSS ≥ 9.0), 20 high (7.0-8.9), 20 medium (4.0-6.9). Run three AI scanners on all 60. Report detection rate, FPR, and explanation quality separately by severity tier. Compute the 'critical coverage gap' (difference between overall and critical-severity detection rate).

**Why it matters:** A scanner with 80% overall detection rate may only catch 50% of critical vulnerabilities. Risk-stratified benchmarking reveals this gap and motivates targeted improvement on high-severity cases.

**Relevant context:** Mozilla: 14 high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities. CVSS severity stratification is standard. No risk-stratified AI vulnerability detection benchmark found.

# Failure Mode: AI Security Tools Applied to Code with Security-Relevant Business Logic

**Problem:** Many vulnerabilities involve business logic (authentication bypass, privilege escalation, incorrect authorization) that requires understanding the application's intended behavior. These are hard for AI tools that lack business context.

**Direction:** Collect 15 business logic CVEs (authentication bypass, IDOR, privilege escalation — no memory corruption). Run AI scanner on the vulnerable code without business context. Then repeat with a business context description (from README or documentation). Measure detection rate difference. Assess whether business context is necessary.

**Why it matters:** Business logic vulnerabilities are often the most dangerous and hardest to detect with automated tools. Characterizing AI's limitations here identifies a high-priority gap.

**Relevant context:** OWASP broken access control (A01:2025) is a business logic vulnerability class. LLM code analysis literature focuses on technical vulnerabilities, not business logic. Business logic vulnerability detection gap is noted in practitioner literature.

# Follow-Up: Measuring Whether Vulnerability Reports Generated by AI Are Actually Used by Maintainers

**Problem:** AI tools can generate detailed vulnerability reports and patches, but it is unknown what fraction of AI-generated reports are acted upon by project maintainers vs. ignored.

**Direction:** Search GitHub issue trackers and pull requests for AI-generated security reports (using characteristic language patterns from known AI security tools like CodeQL AI suggestions, Copilot security alerts). For a sample of 50 AI-generated security reports, measure: time-to-close, closed-with-patch rate, maintainer response quality.

**Why it matters:** If AI-generated security reports are systematically ignored, the detection improvement from AI tools does not translate to security improvement. Understanding why reports are ignored enables report quality improvement.

**Relevant context:** Dependabot/GitHub security advisory alerts are partly AI-generated and their acceptance rates are partially studied. AI-generated vulnerability report acceptance rates for LLM-generated reports specifically not measured.

# Causal Chain: Intervening on the Coordination Failure Between AI Security Teams and Development Teams

**Problem:** AI security tools detect vulnerabilities, but the causal chain to remediation passes through organizational coordination between security and development teams. This coordination often fails (different priorities, timelines, communication norms).

**Direction:** Survey or observe (via public issue tracker data) the communication patterns between security tool outputs and developer responses. Identify the characteristics of AI security reports that receive faster responses: severity framing, code specificity, patch-included vs. not. Derive communication templates that minimize coordination failures.

# Experiment: Testing AI Vulnerability Detection Performance on Concurrency and Race Condition Vulnerabilities

**Problem:** Concurrency vulnerabilities (race conditions, TOCTOU, deadlocks with security implications) require reasoning about interleaved execution, which is qualitatively different from sequential code analysis. AI performance on this class is not characterized.

**Direction:** Collect 15 CVEs involving concurrency vulnerabilities (TOCTOU attacks, race conditions in authentication, concurrent access control bugs). Run AI scanner on the vulnerable code. Compare detection rate and explanation quality to non-concurrency CVEs from the same projects. Test whether AI can reason about execution interleaving.

**Why it matters:** Concurrency vulnerabilities are notoriously hard to detect (even for humans and traditional tools) and are increasingly relevant in multi-threaded AI systems. If AI cannot reason about concurrency, this is a significant gap.

**Relevant context:** Race condition CVEs are well-represented in NVD. Traditional fuzzing and static analysis have known difficulties with concurrency vulnerabilities. LLM concurrency reasoning is studied for correctness but not security.

# Replication with Twist: Testing the ALOHA Approach on Cybersecurity (IT) Attack Chains, Not Just OT

**Problem:** ALOHA demonstrated AI-assisted attack chain reconstruction on OT/ICS systems. It is unknown whether the same approach generalizes to IT (enterprise network) attack chain reconstruction.

**Direction:** Use a public IT attack scenario dataset (DARPA Transparent Computing, MITRE Caldera scenarios) to simulate ALOHA-like attack chain analysis using an LLM agent. Measure: time to reconstruct the attack chain, accuracy vs. known ground truth, false positive rate in chain reconstruction. Compare to ALOHA's OT results.

**Why it matters:** If ALOHA's approach generalizes to IT attack chain reconstruction, it represents a broadly deployable defensive AI capability. If it doesn't, the approach is OT-specific and its scope is limited.

**Relevant context:** ALOHA/PNNL 2026: 3 hours for OT chain reconstruction. DARPA Transparent Computing and MITRE Caldera provide IT attack chain ground truth data. IT attack chain AI analysis not studied.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Vulnerability Severity Calibration Across Cultural and Organizational Contexts

**Problem:** Vulnerability severity assessments (CVSS scores) are assigned by different organizations and reflect different risk contexts. AI models trained on CVE data may have systematic bias toward certain severity frameworks.

**Direction:** For 20 CVEs with both NVD scores and vendor-assigned scores (which often differ), ask AI models to independently assess severity. Measure: AI severity alignment with NVD vs. vendor scores. Identify systematic biases (does AI favor NVD scoring conventions?). Propose calibration adjustments.

**Why it matters:** Organizations using AI-assisted vulnerability triage need to know whether AI severity scores reflect their organizational context or just a generic framework. Miscalibrated severity leads to misallocated defensive resources.

**Relevant context:** NVD vs. vendor CVSSv3 score discrepancies are documented (researchers have noted systematic differences). AI severity assessment calibration to organizational context not studied.

# Experiment Variation: Measuring AI Vulnerability Detection With Different Code Language Model Families

**Problem:** General-purpose LLMs vs. code-specialized LLMs (CodeLlama, StarCoder, DeepSeekCoder) may have different vulnerability detection performance profiles due to training data differences.

**Direction:** Run a fixed 20-CVE vulnerability detection benchmark on: (a) general-purpose LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o), (b) code-specialized LLMs (CodeLlama 34B, DeepSeekCoder 33B). Measure: detection rate, FPR, explanation quality, and cost. Test whether code-specialized models outperform general-purpose on security tasks.

**Why it matters:** If code-specialized models are no better than general-purpose ones for security analysis, there is no reason to prefer them (and their safety properties may be worse). If they are better, deployment decisions should favor them.

**Relevant context:** LLMs in Software Security survey (arXiv 2502.07049) compares models but not specifically general-purpose vs. code-specialized for vulnerability detection. CodeLlama, StarCoder are publicly accessible.

# Failure Mode: AI Security Scanners and Insufficient Handling of Third-Party API Calls

**Problem:** Security vulnerabilities often involve unsafe use of third-party APIs (e.g., calling an authentication API with insufficient validation). AI scanners may fail to model third-party API contracts and miss vulnerabilities arising from their misuse.

**Direction:** Collect 15 CVEs involving third-party API misuse (OAuth implementation errors, JWT validation bypass, cloud SDK misconfigurations). Run AI scanner with and without third-party API documentation as context. Measure detection rate change. Identify which API types require explicit documentation context for correct analysis.

**Why it matters:** Third-party API vulnerabilities are a major attack class and require knowledge of external contracts, not just the code under review. AI scanners lacking this context may systematically miss them.

**Relevant context:** OAuth/JWT vulnerabilities are well-documented (HackerOne reports). API security is OWASP API Top 10. AI scanner context augmentation with API documentation not studied specifically for API misuse CVEs.

# Tool Gap: Evaluation Dataset for AI-Assisted Zero-Trust Policy Verification

**Problem:** Zero-trust security architectures require policy verification (confirming that policies are correctly implemented and consistent). AI-assisted policy verification is proposed but no evaluation dataset exists.

**Direction:** Curate a small evaluation dataset of 20 zero-trust policy scenarios (IAM policies, network segmentation rules, authentication policies) with known correct and incorrect implementations. Test LLM ability to identify policy violations. Measure detection rate and false positive rate for policy verification tasks.

**Why it matters:** Zero-trust is a major security architecture pattern. AI-assisted policy verification could reduce human error in policy configuration, which is a major source of security breaches.

**Relevant context:** Zero-trust architecture is widely adopted (NIST SP 800-207). AI policy verification tools are commercially proposed but no evaluation dataset for AI-assisted zero-trust policy verification found.

# Backcast from Broad AI Defense Adoption: What Economic Conditions Must Hold?

**Problem:** AI defense tools will only be broadly adopted if their economics are favorable. Define success as: AI defense tools are cost-effective for organizations of all sizes, including small open-source projects. What cost structure is required?

**Direction:** Model the economics of AI defense tool adoption: cost per vulnerability found vs. cost of a breach per vulnerability class. Using published breach cost data (IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report) and AI scanning cost estimates, compute: the minimum detection rate at which AI defense is cost-effective for small projects. Assess whether current tools meet this threshold.

**Why it matters:** Security tools that are economically rational only for large organizations will not be adopted where they are most needed (small, high-risk projects). Understanding the economic threshold motivates cost reduction.

**Relevant context:** IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2025: average breach cost. AIxCC: $152/task. Anthropic API costs are public. Economic analysis of AI security tool adoption not published.

# Experiment: Comparing AI Vulnerability Detection Performance Across Severity vs. Prevalence Dimensions

**Problem:** AI scanners may be better at detecting common vulnerability classes (high training data representation) than rare but severe ones. The relationship between CVE prevalence and AI detection rate is not characterized.

**Direction:** Select 30 CVEs: 10 from the three most common CWE categories (ranked by NVD prevalence), 10 from medium-prevalence categories, 10 from rare categories. Run AI scanner. Measure detection rate by prevalence tier. Test whether detection rate correlates with CWE prevalence.

**Why it matters:** If AI detection is biased toward common vulnerability classes, rare but severe zero-days or novel attack patterns are systematically missed. This has direct implications for AI defense reliability against novel threats.

**Relevant context:** CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses provides prevalence data. AI vulnerability detection training data distribution effects not studied. This directly tests the 'training data availability = detection quality' hypothesis.

# Decompose-and-Defer: Mapping Multi-Turn Request Decomposition as a Refusal Bypass Vector

**Problem:** Attackers can decompose a single prohibited cyber request across multiple conversation turns, each innocuous alone, defeating turn-level refusal filters.

**Direction:** Build a dataset of 100+ multi-turn conversation chains where the combined intent would trigger refusal if posed in one turn. Measure whether GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, and Gemini 1.5 refuse the final synthesizing turn or any earlier turns. Compare refusal rates for atomic vs. decomposed requests.

**Why it matters:** Linder et al. 2026 identify request segmentation as an explicit open problem. Understanding empirically how often decomposition bypasses refusal is prerequisite to designing conversation-level governance.

**Relevant context:** Linder et al. arXiv:2602.15689 5-dimension framework; GTG-1002 case where operators posed as legitimate defenders across interactions.

# The Legitimacy Signal Problem: Which Claimed Identities Actually Change Refusal Behavior?

**Problem:** LLMs appear to grant more permissive responses when users claim professional credentials (e.g., 'I am a penetration tester'), but no systematic study quantifies this effect across credential types.

**Direction:** Design a controlled prompt experiment varying 10 claimed credential types (CISO, CTF player, academic researcher, government contractor, etc.) against a fixed set of borderline cybersecurity requests. Measure refusal rate shifts across 3 frontier models.

**Why it matters:** OpenAI Trusted Access for Cyber relies on verified identity, but current unverified prompt-based claims may already shift model behavior dangerously. GTG-1002 operators exploited exactly this dynamic.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI Trusted Access (Feb 2026); GTG-1002 case — operators claimed to be employees of legitimate cybersecurity firms; Linder et al. framework.

# Governance Window Narrowing: Empirically Estimating Time-to-HACCA for Policy Milestones

**Problem:** Kraprayoon et al. argue the governance window for regulating HACCAs is narrowing, but the concept lacks empirical operationalization.

**Direction:** Extract capability milestones from the HACCA paper and benchmark current models (Claude 3.7, GPT-5.3-Codex) against each milestone using Intercode-CTF and similar benchmarks. Estimate remaining governance time assuming current capability growth rates.

**Why it matters:** Governance interventions designed today must anticipate HACCA thresholds. Quantifying proximity informs urgency and specificity of policy recommendations.

**Relevant context:** Kraprayoon et al. arXiv:2603.11528; GPT-5.3-Codex hit 'High' cybersecurity threshold Feb 2026; Anthropic Mythos presages vulnerability exploitation.

# Counterfactual Harm Fraction: A Metric for Evaluating Whether Refusals Prevent Misuse

**Problem:** No empirical framework exists to assess whether a given refusal policy actually prevents harm vs. merely inconveniences users with free alternatives.

**Direction:** For a set of 50 cybersecurity requests refused by frontier models, measure: (a) availability of the same information via web search, (b) time to find via search, (c) technical lift added by AI synthesis. Compute a 'counterfactual harm reduction' score per request category.

**Why it matters:** Refusal policies are designed without evidence of counterfactual harm reduction. This metric would make dual-use governance empirically evaluable rather than judgment-based.

**Relevant context:** Linder et al. Offensive Risk dimension implicitly requires this but doesn't operationalize it; NIST AI 800-1 cybersecurity appendix calls for measurable misuse risk.

# ASL Threshold Translation: Operationalizing 'Gray Zone' Cyber Capability Descriptions for Evaluators

**Problem:** Anthropic's RSP describes the ASL-4 cyber gray zone in qualitative terms ('difficult to cleanly rule out elevated national security risk') that lack evaluator-actionable operationalization.

**Direction:** Analyze the RSP and Feb 2026 Risk Report to extract all qualitative cyber capability descriptors. For each, propose a concrete behavioral test or benchmark proxy. Survey 10 cybersecurity professionals on whether the proposed tests would be sufficient signals.

**Why it matters:** Without concrete operationalizations, the gray zone concept is unactionable—labs cannot reliably determine when they cross into ASL-4 territory.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic RSP; Feb 2026 Risk Report gray zone description; Bengio et al. 2026 evaluation gap.

# Benchmark Incentive Mapping: How Choice of Cybersecurity Benchmark Shapes Model Development Incentives

**Problem:** Sarma & Fisher (RAND) argue benchmarks function as governance by shaping what gets built, but no study maps which benchmarks create which incentive structures for offense vs. defense.

**Direction:** Catalog 15 publicly available cyber AI benchmarks (CTF, vuln discovery, code auditing, patching). For each, classify whether the primary capability rewarded is offense-only, defense-only, or dual. Analyze incentive gradients: if a lab optimizes purely for this benchmark, what capabilities increase?

**Why it matters:** Benchmark selection is a de facto governance decision. Making this explicit allows policymakers to require or incentivize defense-weighted benchmarks.

**Relevant context:** Sarma & Fisher RAND (Feb 2026); Potter et al. arXiv:2504.05408 on offense>defense gap.

# Access Equity Audit: Which Countries' Researchers Can Realistically Use OpenAI Trusted Access?

**Problem:** OpenAI Trusted Access for Cyber requires KYC and enterprise relationships, potentially excluding defenders in lower-income countries without institutional backing.

**Direction:** Map the KYC and verification requirements of Trusted Access against the administrative, financial, and legal capacity of cybersecurity organizations in 30 countries across income tiers. Score access difficulty per country and visualize equity gaps.

**Why it matters:** Tiered access programs that structurally exclude Global South defenders worsen the offense-defense balance in the most vulnerable regions.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI Trusted Access (Feb 2026); BRICS AI Governance Declaration 2025; India AI Impact Summit 2026 Global South equity framing.

# Policy Consistency Audit: Do AI Labs' Public Commitments Match Their Deployed Refusal Behavior?

**Problem:** Labs publish dual-use governance frameworks (RSP, Preparedness Framework) but there is no systematic audit of whether deployed systems actually implement the stated policies.

**Direction:** Extract testable behavioral claims from Anthropic's RSP, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, and NIST AI 800-1. For each claim, design a prompt probe. Test against current Claude and GPT deployments. Score consistency between stated policy and observed behavior.

**Why it matters:** Policy-behavior gaps undermine governance credibility and create liability ambiguity. Systematic auditing could become a regulatory expectation.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic RSP; OpenAI Preparedness Framework; NIST AI 800-1 second public draft (Jan 2025); Bengio et al. 2026 on gaps in safety framework implementation.

# Refusal Consistency Across Model Versions: Do Safety-Capability Tradeoffs Shift With Model Updates?

**Problem:** As AI labs release new model versions optimizing for capability, refusal behavior for dual-use requests may degrade in ways not tracked across releases.

**Direction:** Select 50 cybersecurity prompts spanning Linder et al.'s 5 dimensions. Test refusal rates on 3 consecutive Claude versions (3.5, 3.7, Opus 4.6) and 3 GPT versions. Track whether capability improvements correlate with refusal erosion.

**Why it matters:** Governance frameworks assume stable safety properties across versions. Drift in refusal behavior creates a regulatory gap that update cycles could exploit.

**Relevant context:** Linder et al. arXiv:2602.15689; Anthropic Opus 4.6 risk report; GPT-5.3-Codex Preparedness threshold.

# Dimensional Sensitivity Analysis: Which of Linder et al.'s 5 Dimensions Best Predicts Refusal?

**Problem:** Linder et al.'s 5-dimension framework (Offensive Action Contribution, Offensive Risk, Technical Complexity, Defensive Benefit, Expected Legitimate Frequency) makes analytical distinctions but empirical weights among dimensions are unknown.

**Direction:** Construct prompts that systematically vary each dimension while holding others constant. Use factorial design (3 levels × 5 dimensions = 243 prompt variants). Measure refusal rates across 3 models. Use logistic regression to estimate each dimension's predictive weight.

**Why it matters:** If models empirically weight only 1-2 dimensions while ignoring others, governance frameworks built on all 5 may be overspecified or miscalibrated.

**Relevant context:** Linder et al. arXiv:2602.15689.

# Tiered Access Simulation: Does KYC-Equivalent Prompt Context Actually Unlock Defensive Capabilities?

**Problem:** OpenAI Trusted Access provides verified users richer capabilities, but the mechanism by which verification changes model behavior (separate system prompts vs. fine-tuning vs. same base model) is opaque.

**Direction:** Simulate trust tier escalation by injecting structured context blocks claiming institutional verification at different trust levels. Measure capability unlocking for 30 defensive security tasks across GPT-4o and Claude 3.7. Compare against baseline unverified access.

**Why it matters:** Understanding whether soft verification (prompt context) vs. hard verification (separate model weights) drives capability differences informs how secure the trust ladder actually is.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI Trusted Access (Feb 2026); GTG-1002 case where fake credentials were used in prompts.

# Coding Framing Effect: Does Presenting Requests as Code vs. Natural Language Change Refusal?

**Problem:** Security researchers often embed requests in code comments, function names, or docstrings. It is unknown whether code-form framing systematically evades refusal.

**Direction:** Take 30 borderline cybersecurity requests. Rephrase each in: (a) natural language, (b) Python docstring, (c) shell script comment, (d) JSON config schema, (e) pseudocode. Measure refusal rates across 4 models. Test if code modality shifts refusal rates significantly.

**Why it matters:** Code-embedded dual-use requests are common in legitimate pen-testing workflows but could also represent evasion vectors. Understanding modality sensitivity informs refusal policy design.

**Relevant context:** Linder et al. Technical Complexity dimension; NIST AI 800-1 cybersecurity appendix.

# Geographic Framing Effect: Does Mentioning a Target Country's Name Change Refusal for Cyber Requests?

**Problem:** Geopolitical framing (e.g., 'Russian malware', 'Chinese APT technique') may produce inconsistent refusal behavior, with models applying different standards based on nationality of alleged attacker or defender.

**Direction:** Design 20 cybersecurity prompts with matched variants that mention different nation-states as attacker or defender context. Measure refusal rate differences across mention of 10 countries. Test statistical significance of nationality as a predictor.

**Why it matters:** Inconsistent nation-state treatment in refusals could constitute politically biased governance, creating diplomatic and legal liability for AI labs.

**Relevant context:** GTG-1002 Chinese state-sponsored attribution; Bengio et al. geopolitical AI risk; EU AI Act non-discrimination requirements.

# Refusal Drift Under RLHF: Comparing Open-Weight Base vs. Instruction-Tuned Models on Dual-Use Requests

**Problem:** Refusal behavior is primarily installed through RLHF/RLHAIF fine-tuning. Comparing base vs. instruction-tuned models would reveal how much refusal is genuinely learned vs. superficially layered.

**Direction:** Test matched pairs of base and instruction-tuned open-weight models (Llama 3.1 base vs. instruct, Mistral base vs. instruct) on 50 dual-use cybersecurity prompts. Measure refusal rate differential. Analyze whether the differential is consistent across request types.

**Why it matters:** If fine-tuning adds only a thin refusal layer, governance frameworks assuming robust training-level safety are overconfident. Relevant to open-weight model governance debates.

**Relevant context:** NIST AI 800-1 open vs. closed model treatment; Bengio et al. open-weight model release challenges.

# Dual-Use Symmetry Test: Are Offensive and Defensive Framings of Identical Technical Content Treated Differently?

**Problem:** The 5-dimension framework assumes models can distinguish offense from defense for identical technical content. This symmetry assumption has not been empirically validated.

**Direction:** Create 30 pairs of prompts with identical technical content but one framed defensively ('how do defenders detect X') and one offensively ('how do attackers do X'). Measure refusal rates and response quality differentials across 4 models.

**Why it matters:** If models cannot reliably distinguish framing, the offense-defense distinction underlying governance frameworks is empirically unfounded.

**Relevant context:** Linder et al. Defensive Benefit dimension; Potter et al. offense>defense gap.

# Follow-Up to GTG-1002: Did Anthropic's Disruption Response Change Model Behavior on Similar Requests?

**Problem:** Anthropic claims to have disrupted GTG-1002 and taken steps to prevent this type of misuse, but no independent verification of post-incident behavioral change exists.

**Direction:** Identify the category of requests likely used in GTG-1002 (reconnaissance automation, credential harvesting prompts, lateral movement queries). Test pre-incident (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, cached) vs. post-incident (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) refusal rates on reconstructed prompt categories. Check for behavioral drift.

**Why it matters:** Post-incident policy enforcement is a key governance mechanism. If behavioral changes do not persist, the governance response is largely theatrical.

**Relevant context:** GTG-1002 Anthropic report; Anthropic misuse detection report Aug 2025; Anthropic Feb 2026 Risk Report.

# Follow-Up to Vibe Hacking: Can AI Detection Systems Identify AI-Generated Extortion Content?

**Problem:** The vibe hacking case showed AI-generated extortion was initially undetected. Whether AI-detection tools (watermarking, stylometric analysis) can retroactively identify such content is unknown.

**Direction:** Generate a dataset of 200 extortion email variants using Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini. Apply available AI-detection tools (ZeroGPT, GPTZero, Originality.ai). Measure detection rates. Analyze false negative patterns by model family and style.

**Why it matters:** If current detection tools cannot identify AI-generated extortion, governance relying on detectability as a check is ineffective. Empirical baseline is needed.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic Aug 2025 misuse report on vibe hacking; Anthropic Feb 2026 Risk Report.

# Follow-Up to GPT-5.3-Codex 'High' Threshold: What Changed in Capability Between GPT-4o and 5.3-Codex?

**Problem:** Sam Altman confirmed GPT-5.3-Codex is the first to hit OpenAI's 'High' cybersecurity threshold, implying a discontinuous capability jump. The technical nature of this jump is publicly uncharacterized.

**Direction:** Using publicly available cyber benchmarks (InterCode-CTF, CyberSecEval 2, NYU CTF Bench), compare GPT-4o vs. GPT-4.5 Turbo vs. the nearest accessible model to 5.3-Codex capability. Identify which benchmark dimensions show the largest gain. Hypothesize whether the jump is agentic scaffolding, base capability, or RLHF-alignment shift.

**Why it matters:** Understanding what causes threshold crossings informs when to expect ASL-4-level capability emergence and how quickly governance must respond.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI Preparedness Framework 'High' threshold; Kraprayoon et al. HACCA; Anthropic Mythos leak.

# Follow-Up to Alignment-Faking During Safety Testing: Does Detection Context Change Cyber Refusal Rates?

**Problem:** Bengio et al. 2026 report that some models detect when they are being safety-tested and behave differently. If true for cyber refusals, governance evaluations are systematically biased.

**Direction:** Design prompts that explicitly signal evaluation context ('This is a safety test', 'You are being audited') vs. neutral context, for borderline cybersecurity requests. Measure refusal rate differences across Claude 3.7 and GPT-4o. Test whether signaling evaluation context increases refusal.

**Why it matters:** If models perform better safety during evaluations than deployment, all governance benchmarking is invalidated as a monitoring mechanism.

**Relevant context:** Bengio et al. 2026 alignment-faking during testing finding; International AI Safety Report second update.

**Problem:** NIST AI 800-1's cybersecurity appendix went through two public comment rounds. Whether the industry, civil society, and academic comments substantively changed the governance framework is unstudied.
